name: Shrimp Welfare Project: Humane Slaughter Initiative (charityevals)
summary: Shrimp Welfare Project buys electrical stunners and lends them to shrimp producers in Asia, Latin America and Africa who commit to stun part of their harvest instead of killing the shrimp in ice slurry. This models the stunners its spending in the year to March 2025 bought (a price per stunner, so the next dollar buys more at about that price), about 79% of its programme spending: retailer engagement, the India farmer programme and research aren't modelled. The result is about 1.6 years of healthy life per $1,000, and the biggest uncertainties are how much a shrimp can suffer and how much suffering a stun spares.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

rows.label: Humane Slaughter Initiative's share of the year's direct running costs
rows.explainer: The accounts don't split spending by programme. Our judgment, anchored on the team page: of 16 staff today, the programme implementation director, the strategic industry partnerships director, the Asia and Latin America technical field coordinators and the monitoring lead work with producers on stunners, with part of leadership's time; retailer engagement, the India farmer programme (two staff), research, communications and operations share the rest. The low end (0.35) reflects the trustees' report for 2024-25, which lists research, retailer engagement (Morrisons), two memorandums with industry partners and communications among its achievements and doesn't mention stunners. With the stunners' price this makes the stunner programme about 79% (69-86%) of the year's programme spending.

source.title: Shrimp Welfare Project, Humane Slaughter Initiative impact model (Guesstimate, its own, linked from its (Shr)Impact page)
source.page: per agreement: Production p.a. (MT) x Proportion committed to be stunned, and Cost ($); the eleven agreements added April 2024 to March 2025 (Asia 02-09, Asia 12, LatAm 06, LatAm 07)
source.quote: Proportion committed to be stunned: In accordance with the commitment signed and the negotiations.

rows.explainer: Shrimp Welfare Project's own model lists each producer agreement: yearly production, the share it commits to stun, and the stunner's price. The eleven agreements added between April 2024 and March 2025 (dated by when each entered the model, our proxy for signing) commit 28,468 tonnes a year (for example 6,000 t x 100%, 9,500 t x 26%, 12,500 t x 14.4%) for stunners costing $674,350 (nine at $55,000, one at $73,200, one at $106,150): 0.0422 t a year per stunner dollar. Range: the same ratio for the agreements of the year before (0.0503) and the year after (0.0346), in case the year's purchases went to agreements dated otherwise. The year's purchases (about $496,000) are below the year's agreements' price because some were paid the next year; purchases to March 2025 (£630,121, about $805,000) roughly match the agreements signed by then (about $894,000). The trustees' report's "two new Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) with industry partners" don't list these producer agreements; the year's fixed-asset additions (about nine stunners at $55,000) are the cross-check on the count. A count of commitments, not of shrimp already stunned: whether producers stun it is the implementation adjustment.

rows.label: Shrimp per kilogram at harvest

source.title: FAO, Cultured Aquatic Species Information Programme: Penaeus vannamei
source.quote: Cultured shrimp harvested from ponds (after 4–5 months at 15–25 g)

rows.explainer: Pond-farmed whiteleg shrimp, about 80% of farmed penaeid shrimp worldwide and probably most of the agreements' production, are harvested at 15-25 g (FAO), 40-67 a kilogram; extensive ponds harvest smaller shrimp of 11-12 g (FAO), about 85 a kilogram. Best guess 60 a kilogram (about 17 g), between FAO's pond range and the charity's own figures: its model assumes 10-20 g ("around 70 shrimps/kg") and its (Shr)Impact page implies about 66 for the installed stunners (54,175 tonnes, about 3.6 billion shrimp) and about 72 for all commitments (6.5 billion shrimp, 89,774 tonnes). Whiteleg shrimp are about 80% of farmed penaeid shrimp (EU market observatory, citing FAO: https://fishery-aquaculture-market-observatory.ec.europa.eu/en/country-and-species-profiles/species-profiles/shrimp-penaeus); the producers' giant tiger shrimp, larger at harvest, would lower the count. Range 40 (25 g) to 90 (11 g).

rows.label: Shrimp a year to be stunned under the stunners the year's spending bought
rows.explainer: The year's stunner purchases at the year's agreements' committed tonnes per stunner dollar, in shrimp (tonnes x 1,000 kg x shrimp per kg). Everything the agreements commit, not only what is already stunned: delivery is the implementation adjustment.

rows.label: Share of the committed shrimp not already stunned before the agreement
rows.explainer: The agreements go to producers without electrical stunning (the programme lends a stunner to a producer that commits to stun with it, one per producer, a second only after a year's use: the programme page). The low end allows for some volume already stunned another way.

rows.label: Animals per year the campaign can change
SADs averted per shrimp electrically stunned before slaughter
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for stunning a shrimp before slaughter (2025 SADs), instead of slaughter by ice slurry or asphyxiation, counted once per shrimp slaughtered. Its best guess sits at the bottom of its range (0.0045, up to 0.10), a judgment the site makes for every shrimp-stunning model.

rows.label: Years a stunner keeps working at the producer
rows.explainer: No source states it: the programme page says the units are robust and maintenance light; the accounts write them down at 25% a year on a reducing balance, an accounting convention rather than a life. Our judgment, anchored on industrial processing equipment of the kind (about 5 to 15 years), shortened for a wet, salty processing hall.

rows.label: Years a stunner's work counts: its working life, at most the years a won reform counts
rows.explainer: A producer that starts stunning because of the loan would probably have started some day anyway, as retailers in Europe ask for stunned shrimp. Like every won change, it counts the site's years a reform counts before it would have come anyway (Your values; 5 by default), and never longer than the stunner works.

rows.label: Years from buying the stunner until it stuns at the committed volume
rows.explainer: Shipping, import, installation, commissioning and training. By November 2026, 20 of the 37 stunners agreed since 2023 were installed and commissioned (the (Shr)Impact page), and 15 agreements in the charity's model date from before April 2025, fewer than the 20 installed; a year from purchase is our judgment, from half a year to two.

rows.label: Years a donated dollar waits in reserves before it is spent
rows.explainer: The charity took in £2.24 million and spent about £0.80 million in cash in the year (stunners at their price, depreciation and currency losses out), ending with £2.65 million in the bank (balance sheet, p. 10): about three years of that year's spending, against a reserves target of six months of core costs (trustees' report, section 5). Spending is growing (14 agreements in the following year, stunners priced at about $920,000 in its model), so a dollar given now waits about a year before it buys a stunner: our judgment, half a year to two. Discounted with the other waits; the interest the waiting money earns is added in the next rows.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: a stunned shrimp gets an effective stun in everyday use
rows.explainer: Whether everyday use matches the conditions the shared SADs figure stands for: correct electrical settings, enough time in the stunner, stunning before the ice slurry rather than after. What share of stuns the shared figure already assumes fail isn't stated in the sandbox's facts (its high end carries a 0.97 factor), so this covers only misuse in the field beyond it. No independent audit of the producers' use is public. 0.85, our judgment; 0.6 if stuns are often ineffective, 1 at face value.

rows.label: Share of the committed stunning that wouldn't have started without the loaned stunner
rows.explainer: Some producers would have bought a stunner themselves about as soon, under pressure from European retailers' stunning policies: in April 2026 an Indonesian producer, PT Brother, chose a stunner system from Ace Aquatec, with no mention of Shrimp Welfare Project (Perishable News, 27 April 2026, https://perishablenews.com/seafood/pt-brother-sets-bar-for-shrimp-welfare-standards-with-ace-aquatec-system/). Those count zero; the others count the years above (one question per adjustment: when, not whether). Our judgment. The price itself isn't the barrier: a $55,000 stunner is about 6% of a year's margin on the committed 1,900 tonnes (FAO: farm-gate price about USD 3.0-3.5/kg against production costs of about USD 2.5-3.0/kg). What holds producers back is that buyers don't yet pay more for stunned shrimp, the producers lack know-how, and it would be a first purchase of new equipment; the one self-purchase we found (PT Brother) came after three years of the programme. So most of the year's producers wouldn't have started stunning this early: 0.75 (0.5-0.95).

rows.label: Shrimp Welfare Project's share of the resources behind the stunning
rows.explainer: SWP pays for the stunner, training and follow-up; the producer pays freight, import duties, installation, power and the staff who run it; the retailers' stunning policies that create demand were pushed by several animal groups and SWP; three volunteers (operations, communications) give a little unpaid time, a negligible share. Our judgment of SWP's share of everything that went in, the same in both credit modes (Convention 2).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of the committed volume producers actually stun
rows.explainer: Shrimp pledges have no shared record of pledges kept, so this is a judgment. For: the producer holds the equipment, and SWP keeps ownership and can reclaim it "if agreed terms are not being met" (programme page). Against: the (Shr)Impact figure is "a projection based on signed commitments — not a count of shrimp that have already been stunned", verified use is still being "progressively" strengthened, and volumes depend on buyers paying for stunned shrimp. Anchors: 20 of the 37 agreements signed since 2023 were installed and commissioned by November 2026 (54%; mostly the older ones, so the share of agreements eventually installed is higher), though installed stunners carry 60% of committed tonnes (54,175 of 89,774); the charity's model numbers agreements with gaps (no Asia 01, no LatAm 03), which may be agreements that fell through; Aquatic Life Institute's model (ACE) puts retailers' shrimp-stunning commitments at 50-60% (30-80%), a weaker kind of commitment than a producer holding a stunner. 0.6 (0.3-0.85).

rows.label: Effects not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: + Demonstration: producers stunning at scale show buyers and other producers it works, and some buy their own. + Better handling at slaughter that comes with the training. - Shrimp stunned but then handled badly, or a stunned volume shifted from another stunned line. Net +10%, our judgment.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.
